She never really wanted to know. She only ever wanted to become something worth glowing for.

perStory.premise: A city wakes up one day to discover every person's
perStory.text:
The city woke up already looking away from itself.

Mara noticed it first on the subway platform, in the space above people's heads, where a kind of subtitle hovered—faint, gray, legible only if you looked directly at someone. The man beside her was thinking *I hope she doesn't smell the wine on my breath from last night.* The woman across the platform was thinking, in a loop, *not late not late not late.* Nobody was saying anything about it out loud yet, because everybody was too busy reading everybody else, and too afraid of what was being read off them in turn.

By nine a.m. the streets had gone quiet in a new way. People walked with their eyes down, not on their phones now but on the pavement, as if the sidewalk itself might stop broadcasting if they refused to look up. The coffee shop on Ninth had a line that moved in total silence except for one woman who kept saying "sorry, sorry" to no one, because her thoughts—*ugly, ugly, why did I wear this, everyone can see*—kept scrolling above her head like a marquee she couldn't switch off.

Mara worked at a insurance office on the eleventh floor. Her supervisor, Denny, stood at the front of the morning huddle with a thought hanging over him in soft gray letters: *I don't know how to do this job either, I never have.* Nobody had known that about Denny. Denny, who wrote memos in a font so confident it felt like a threat. People looked at him differently the rest of the day, and by lunch, gently, without meaning to, they had begun trusting him more.

That was the first strange mercy of it.

The second came at noon, when Mara's ex-husband texted asking if they could talk. She almost didn't go, until she remembered, with a small shock, that she could simply look at him. So she met him at the corner diner and sat down and looked, and above his head, wavering like heat off asphalt, was *I still don't know how to say I'm sorry without making it about me.* Not a lie. Not a performance. Just the plain unimproved thing, the thing he'd never once managed to say to her in nine years of marriage. She started crying in the booth, not from grief this time but from something more like relief, the relief of not having to guess anymore.

Not everyone found mercy in it. By afternoon there were reports of fights breaking out—a man on the corner of Elm and Ninth had been beaten badly after his thoughts, projected plain as a movie marquee, turned out to be about the woman walking her dog past his stoop every morning. Bank tellers were sent home when customers' thoughts about them curdled the air into something unbearable. Radio hosts begged listeners not to act on what they read above strangers' heads, then broke down on air themselves when their own thoughts—petty, frightened, human—scrolled out for the whole city to see.

By evening, City Hall issued a statement composed, absurdly, entirely of what the mayor was actually thinking, since nobody could figure out how to write around it: *We don't know why this is happening. We don't know how to fix it. I am scared and so is everyone in this room and I don't want to lose the election over something I can't control.* It was, people agreed later, the most honest thing a mayor had ever said.

Mara walked home at dusk through streets grown strange with tenderness and violence in equal measure—a couple weeping quietly on a bench because they'd both, it turned out, been thinking of leaving; two teenagers laughing themselves sick because their thoughts about a shared crush were identically ridiculous; a man crossing the street just to avoid reading anyone at all.

She let herself into her apartment and stood at the window, watching the gray words rise off the city like steam off a river in winter, thousands of unfinished sentences nobody had chosen to say. She wondered whether by morning it would end, and whether, if it did, anyone would remember to keep saying the things out loud that today they hadn't had a choice about.

Above her own head, unseen by her, hung the plain and only thought she'd had all day: *I hope this doesn't stop before I get to tell her.*

She picked up her phone and called her mother.

perStory.premise: The world's luck is finite, and someone has begun
perStory.text:
The luck ledger read zero-point-three-one when Maren checked it that morning, and she almost didn't notice, because the number moved so rarely that most people had stopped looking. It had held steady near one for eleven years — the number the actuaries at the Bureau of Global Fortune had settled on after the Reckoning, when everyone finally agreed the world's luck was a fixed and countable thing, drawn down by every near-miss and every impossible catch, replenished slow as oil.

Point-three-one meant something was wrong. Point-three-one, extrapolated, meant the world ran out of luck in nine days.

She was a fortune auditor, third tier, which meant she watched dials and flagged anomalies for people more important than her, and in eleven years she had flagged nothing, because nothing had ever moved. Now she sat in her cubicle in Geneva watching the number tick down in increments too small to see and too large to ignore, point-three-one becoming point-three-zero-nine, and she did the thing she was trained to never do alone. She traced the draw.

Luck theft left a signature, the training manuals said, a directional pull, like water finding a drain. She built the vector by hand, cross-referencing catastrophe-averted logs against unclaimed windfalls, plotting where luck should have landed and hadn't. The line she drew went east, then south, then converged, over eleven hours of work, on a single tower in Manila, floor forty, a private trading desk registered to a man named Costa Ibarra who had not lost a single position in four years.

Not one. Four years. In a market. That wasn't skill. That was withdrawal.

She flew there herself, because the report would take a week to move through channels and channels moved slower than a man could drain a planet dry. She found Ibarra's office at 2 a.m., paid a cleaner to let her in, and found in the back room not a computer but a wheel — an actual wheel, hand-built, brass and bone, wired into a lattice of copper filament that hummed even unplugged, even in the dark, like it was still eating.

He was there. He hadn't gone home in three days, he told her, because the wheel needed watching now, it was accelerating on its own, feeding on its own draw the way a fire feeds on the wind it makes.

"I didn't build this to hurt anyone," he said. "I built it because I was tired of losing. Do you understand what that's like? Being unlucky your whole life, watching everyone else's coin land right?"

"You emptied the tank for everyone else to fill your own cup."

"I only took the overflow."

"There's no overflow left. You saw the number."

He had, and it had frightened him more than he'd expected, enough that he let her look, enough that between them they found the release valve was a single filament, the first one he'd soldered, load-bearing for the whole apparatus. Cut it and the wheel would either stop or unravel entirely, dump everything back at once, which the manuals said could be its own catastrophe — four years of stolen fortune returning to the world in one convulsive instant, luck as flood instead of luck as tide.

"Slow bleed instead," she said. "We meter it back out. It'll take longer than it took you to steal it."

"How much longer."

"Longer than either of us live, probably."

He looked at the wheel like a father looking at a fire he'd started, and nodded, and together they began the unglamorous work of giving it back — not a decision, not a single brave cut, but a dial turned down one careful notch at a time, for the rest of that night and, though neither of them said it aloud, for the rest of their lives, watching a number climb toward one so slowly that no one else would ever know how close it had come to zero, or how ordinary the reason had been.

perStory.premise: Every dream leaves behind a physical object by mor
perStory.text:
The dream left behind a spoon.

It sat on Marisol's nightstand at 6:14 a.m., catching the gray window light — not one of her spoons, thinner in the neck, bowl slightly too shallow, as if made by someone who had heard spoons described but never held one. She hadn't dreamed of a spoon. She'd dreamed of her grandmother's kitchen in Guadalajara, tiles the color of a bruise, and a conversation she couldn't now remember the words of, only the feeling of being forgiven for something.

This was the forty-first object. She kept them in a shoebox under the bed, because the news had said not to throw them away, not until the scientists understood what they were, though eleven months in nobody understood anything. A brass button. A child's shoe, size 4, never worn. A key that opened nothing she owned. A pinecone that smelled faintly of her father's aftershave, though her father had never been in the dream that produced it, or so she thought — she could never be sure what a dream had actually contained, only what it left on the nightstand like a receipt for a purchase she hadn't agreed to make.

The world had adjusted the way it adjusts to everything, with think pieces and then merchandise and then indifference. There were dream-object appraisers now, on television, holding up a stranger's stone or spool of thread and speculating about its emotional provenance. There were people who dreamed on purpose, chasing objects, drinking melatonin and reciting the name of someone they wanted to see again, waking to nothing, or worse, waking to a paperclip, a single ordinary paperclip, when they'd hoped for a photograph, a lock of hair, some evidence that the dead were still composing themselves somewhere and sending word.

Marisol picked up the spoon and weighed it in her palm. It was warm, they were always faintly warm for the first hour, cooling at the rate of a fresh loaf of bread. She thought of her grandmother's hands, how they'd smelled of cumin no matter how many times they were washed, and she wondered if the spoon was a fragment of an actual spoon that had existed in that kitchen thirty years ago, worn thin by soup and stirred beans, or if it was something newer — a spoon made only for this, manufactured overnight by whatever factory of the unconscious produced these things, shipped across the border between sleep and the waking room with no invoice, no explanation.

Her husband found the objects boring, or said he did, though she'd caught him once turning the little brass button over and over between his fingers with a concentration that looked like grief. He never dreamed of anything, or never remembered it, and so he woke to nothing, every morning, an empty nightstand, and she had begun to suspect this was its own kind of object — an absence with weight, something he carried into the kitchen and set down nowhere, all day.

She put the spoon in the shoebox with the others, sliding it in beside the pinecone so it wouldn't scratch the key. Forty-one now. If she lived to seventy, at this rate, she calculated it out sometimes, doing the arithmetic instead of sleeping — she would have some fourteen thousand objects by the end, a museum of a life's unconscious, more objects than days she could account for, and she wondered who would go through the shoeboxes when she was gone, whether her daughter would understand that the pinecone meant something, that the shoe with no matching foot had cost her a week of sleepless nights trying to remember whose it was.

Downstairs the coffee maker clicked on. Outside, a truck idled, and somewhere in the building a neighbor's alarm went off, muffled, insistent, the ordinary business of a Tuesday continuing regardless.

She closed the shoebox and pushed it back under the bed with her foot, the way you'd close a door on a room you weren't ready to finish furnishing, and went down to make breakfast for a family that, lately, she was no longer sure she recognized fully awake.

perStory.premise: A mountain slowly walks across the continent once
perStory.text:
The mountain's name, in the language of the people who first mapped its passage, meant simply "the one who is late for nothing."

It had crossed the continent eleven times since the first town kept records, and each crossing took nine hundred and eighty-some years, which is to say that no single generation ever saw it arrive and leave. They only ever saw one or the other. Old Yvette Marchetti, who kept the ledger in the valley town of Corvel, was the seventh generation of Marchettis to inherit the duty of watching, and she was the first in three hundred years to actually see it move.

It did not look like movement. That was the trouble with telling anyone. The mountain — they called it Sorrowback, for the long saddle-shaped ridge that dipped like a spine bowed under weight — occupied the eastern horizon the way it always had, a gray-blue tooth against the sky, snow-capped even in August. You could watch it for a hundred years and see nothing but the ordinary theater of weather: clouds snagging on its shoulders, light sliding down its face at dusk. The movement lived underneath that, the way a held breath lives underneath a still chest.

Yvette measured it the way her grandmother had taught her, and her grandmother's grandmother before that: a brass rod driven into bedrock at the edge of the north field, and every solstice, a mark scratched at the place where the mountain's silhouette crossed a notch filed into the rod's head. The marks going back three centuries formed a crooked little ladder, each rung a hair's width from the last. In her lifetime alone, she watched the mountain's shadow crawl four notches westward, and on the day she understood what that meant — that Sorrowback was not just old and unmoving but old and *walking*, the way a glacier walks, the way a held note eventually becomes silence — she sat down in the wet grass and cried, though she could not entirely say why.

There were theories. The old priests said the mountain was a sleeping god shrugging in its sleep. The surveyors from the capital said it was a trick of erosion and tectonic creep, nothing mystical, just impossibly slow geology dressed up in local superstition, though none of their instruments had ever produced a mechanism that explained a solid granite massif relocating itself six hundred miles in a millennium without leaving so much as a scar in the rock behind it — no trench, no rubble field, no bruise on the land where a mountain's foot might have been. It simply was here, and then, generations later, it was somewhere else, and the ground it had stood on healed over like water closing above a stone.

The animals always knew first. Twenty years before an arrival was due, the elk stopped denning on the leeward slopes. The old dogs of Corvel, the ones with some wolf still folded into their blood, took to howling at the saddle ridge on clear nights for no reason their owners could see. And the trees at the mountain's base, Yvette's grandmother swore, grew their rings thin and anxious on the western side, as if bracing.

Yvette was sixty-one when she made her final mark on the brass rod, and she wrote in the ledger, in a hand gone unsteady, that she believed the mountain would not fully arrive in Corvel's sky for another one hundred and forty years, would not stand directly overhead crushing their morning sun into a permanent dusk for another four hundred after that, and would not finish its slow transit west, leaving them behind the way it had left a hundred towns behind before, for six centuries more. She would not see any of it. Her daughter would not. Perhaps no one whose name was already spoken would.

But she made the mark anyway, filed the notch, oiled the rod against rust, and left instructions for her daughter to do the same at the next solstice, and the one after that, on and on, an unbroken chain of small attentive gestures aimed at a thing too large and too slow to notice being watched.

That was the strange mercy of it, she thought, walking back to the house in the dark with the brass rod's cold still on her palms. The mountain did not know it was seen. It did not know it was loved, or feared, or measured in notches by generations of women with the same stubborn jaw. It simply went on crossing the world at the pace the world itself was made to bear, patient as a season, indifferent as tide, and somewhere far behind it, in the lands it had already left, the grass was growing back over the place where a mountain used to be, and no one there remembered anymore that it ever had.
